title: LensBridge: Frequency-Guided Compound Degradation Adaptation for Lens Aberration Correction and Veiling Glare Removal

paper.title: LensBridge: Frequency-Guided Compound Degradation Adaptation for Lens Aberration Correction and Veiling Glare Removal
paper.abstract: Abstract Simplified optical systems often exhibit residual lens aberrations and Veiling Glare (VG), resulting in spatially varying blur and contrast reduction. Large-scale Lens Libraries (LensLib) enable reusable aberration correction models by covering diverse Point Spread Functions (PSFs), but their aberration-only training distribution does not include target-specific veiling glare. Extending such foundations to compound degradation is challenging because realistic target-system compound pairs are difficult to obtain. To address this challenge, we propose LensBridge , a two-stage framework that first establishes a reusable aberration correction foundation and then adapts it to compound optical degradation using only a few unpaired target observations. In Stage I, we build a PSF-aware one-step diffusion foundation by constructing discrete degradation priors from LensLib PSFs and learning to retrieve them directly from aberrated images, enabling PSF-aware correction without requiring explicit PSF at inference. In Stage II, we adapt this foundation to compound degradation through frequency-domain guidance. Our analysis suggests that aberrations affect a broad frequency range, whereas additional veiling glare exhibits stronger low-frequency amplitude variations, motivating a shared target-domain Fourier-amplitude statistic. At the data level, Frequency-guided Degradation Completion (FDC) transfers target low-frequency characteristics to LensLib aberrated images while preserving aberration structures to synthesize compound training pairs; at the model level, Frequency-guided Pseudo Decomposition (FPD) forms aberration- and VG-dominant pseudo observations to condition separate adaptation branches. Extensive experiments across multiple optical systems demonstrate that LensBridge effectively extends reusable aberration correction foundations to joint aberration correction and veiling glare removal without target-system paired supervision. All code will be available at https://github.com/XiaolongQian/LensBridge .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Simplified optical designs enable compact imaging systems for mobile photography ( Chen et al., 2021a ; Chen et al., 2023 ) and emerging meta-optical devices ( Li et al., 2021b ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , but often leave substantial residual lens aberrations. Meanwhile, surface imperfections and non-ideal coatings can also induce diffuse stray-light scattering, manifested as Veiling Glare (VG) ( Qian et al., 2026b ) . Lens aberrations introduce spatially varying blur and chromatic dispersion, while veiling glare causes diffuse luminance contamination and contrast reduction. Their coexistence results in compound optical degradation , motivating computational restoration capable of addressing both effects. Existing computational restoration for optical degradation has primarily focused on lens aberrations. Conventional learning-based approaches typically rely on target-system synthetic pairs generated from Point Spread Functions (PSFs) ( Chen et al., 2021a ; Chen et al., 2021b ) . As illustrated by the synthetic-to-real paradigm in Fig. 1 (a), such models are trained on target-lens synthetic data and then transferred to real aberrated images ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Acquiring target-lens PSFs and constructing synthetic training pairs for new optical system make deployment costly. Pretraining on large-scale Lens Libraries (LensLib) alleviates this burden by learning reusable correction models across diverse aberration distributions ( Gong et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2026a ) . Among these methods, OmniLens ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) follows the foundation-to-specific paradigm in Fig. 1 (a), adapting a LensLib foundation to unseen lenses with unpaired aberrated images and a dark-channel prior. Figure 1: Motivation for LensBridge . (a) Comparison of optical adaptation paradigms in terms of source pretraining and target degradation. LensBridge adapts a reusable aberration correction foundation to target compound degradation using only unpaired target images. (b) In the illustrated example, aberration induces broadband amplitude changes, whereas the additional veiling glare produces predominantly low-frequency amplitude changes and a smaller phase-swap reconstruction error in the illustrated example, motivating the frequency-guided designs of FDC and FPD. However, these reusable foundations are learned within the aberration-only degradation space of LensLib and therefore cannot account for veiling glare. Extending them to compound degradation remains challenging, as physically accurate veiling glare simulation requires optomechanical models and computationally expensive non-sequential ray tracing ( Raskar et al., 2008 ; Hullin et al., 2011 ) , making reliable target-system compound pairs difficult to obtain. A recent solution is target-specific compound degradation synthesis. DeVeiler ( Qian et al., 2026b ) follows the target-specific-to-compound paradigm in Fig. 1 (a), using target-lens aberration pairs and unpaired compound observations to synthesize realistic lens-specific compound degradations for joint restoration. However, its synthesis remains tailored to each target system rather than reusing an aberration correction foundation across lenses. In contrast, we pursue a foundation-to-compound paradigm, where reusable aberration knowledge is retained from LensLib and only a few unpaired compound observations are required to adapt the foundation to a new optical system. To enable such adaptation, we examine the two degradation mechanisms in the frequency domain, where PSF-induced blur and diffuse stray-light effects exhibit different spectral responses. PSF-induced aberration modifies image content across a broad frequency range, whereas veiling glare primarily affects low-frequency amplitude components, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (b). This distinction motivates using target-domain low-frequency amplitude statistics to characterize the degradation information missing from the aberration-only foundation. We therefore propose LensBridge , a two-stage framework that first establishes a reusable aberration correction foundation and then adapts it to compound optical degradation. In Stage I, we establish a PSF-aware one-step diffusion foundation for reusable aberration correction. LensLib PSFs are encoded into a discrete degradation prior space, while image-conditioned retrieval enables the corresponding priors to be inferred directly from aberrated observations. The retrieved priors condition the diffusion restoration backbone, retaining PSF-aware degradation guidance without requiring explicit PSFs at inference. In Stage II, we adapt this foundation to target compound degradation using only a few unpaired target observations. Based on the above frequency distinction, we estimate a shared target-system Fourier-amplitude statistic to guide adaptation at both the data and model levels. At the data level, Frequency-guided Degradation Completion (FDC) performs data-level adaptation by transferring target-domain low-frequency degradation characteristics to LensLib aberrated images while preserving their aberration-related structures and clean counterparts, thereby constructing target-like compound training pairs without learning an additional degradation generator. At the model level, Frequency-guided Pseudo Decomposition (FPD) uses the same frequency statistic to construct aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations, allowing the two adaptation branches to model their distinct degradation characteristics separately. Together, FDC provides target-like training supervision, while FPD separately conditions the aberration and VG adaptation branches. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose LensBridge , a two-stage framework that first establishes a reusable LensLib-based aberration correction foundation and then adapts it to compound aberration and veiling-glare degradation using only a few unpaired target observations. • We introduce FDC and FPD, which leverage a shared target-domain Fourier-amplitude statistic to construct target-like compound training pairs and aberration-/VG-dominant pseudo observations, respectively. • Extensive experiments across multiple optical systems demonstrate the effectiveness of LensBridge for joint aberration correction and veiling glare removal.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Lens Aberration Correction. Computational Aberration Correction (CAC) aims to restore images degraded by residual lens aberrations. Early approaches relied on deconvolution or PSF-based inverse filtering ( Wiener, 1949 ; Fish et al., 1995 ; Schuler et al., 2012 ) . With the emergence of deep learning, learning-based CAC methods ( Chen et al., 2021a ; Chen et al., 2021b ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Mandal et al., 2025 ) learn restoration mappings from simulated optical degradations and achieve improved performance. However, these methods typically depend on lens-specific simulation pipelines and suffer from limited generalization to unseen optical systems. Recent works explore reusable CAC models through large-scale lens library pre-training ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2026a ) , where diverse aberration distributions improve cross-lens generalization and support adaptation to new lenses. Nevertheless, existing LensLib-based frameworks remain confined to PSF-induced aberrations and do not address compound degradations involving veiling glare. Veiling Glare Removal. Veiling glare is a diffuse degradation caused by stray-light scattering inside optical systems, leading to luminance contamination and contrast reduction. Unlike lens flare, which typically appears as localized structures such as bright spots and streaks ( Wu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Dai et al., 2024 ; Vasluianu et al., 2024 ; Zhu & Lee, 2025 ) , veiling glare is spatially distributed and dominated by low-frequency variations. Traditional approaches rely on physical modeling or image decomposition, including Glare Spread Function (GSF) based inverse filtering ( Talvala et al., 2007 ) and glare-component decomposition ( Zhang et al., 2018b ) , but often require restrictive assumptions, calibration, or multiple observations. Recent data-driven methods ( Shoshin & Shvets, 2021 ) use simplified flare or scattering models for training-data synthesis, leaving a substantial gap from lens-specific real degradations. DeVeiler ( Qian et al., 2026b ) addresses this limitation through target-specific compound degradation synthesis, but its degradation modeling must be repeated for each new optical system. In contrast, LensBridge reuses a LensLib-based aberration correction foundation and adapts it to compound degradation using only unpaired target observations. Frequency-Guided Degradation Adaptation. Frequency-domain statistics have been widely explored for domain adaptation and image restoration. FDA transfers low-frequency Fourier amplitudes between source and target domains for unsupervised semantic segmentation ( Yang & Soatto, 2020 ) , while FCA exploits frequency consistency to reduce the synthetic-to-real gap in real-world super-resolution ( Ji et al., 2021 ) . Frequency-aware dehazing methods further exploit amplitude-spectrum discrepancies between synthetic and real degradations for adaptation or restoration ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . These methods demonstrate the effectiveness of frequency statistics for characterizing domain shifts, but mainly use them for global source-to-target alignment or adaptation within a single degradation type. In contrast, LensBridge uses an aggregated target-domain Fourier-amplitude statistic to complete the missing target degradation characteristics associated with VG while preserving the existing LensLib aberration structure, and further reuses the same statistic to construct aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: We aim to recover a latent clean image I c I_{c} from a compound-degraded image I d ​ e I_{de} captured by a target optical system. Following ( Qian et al., 2026b ) , we model the joint effects of spatially varying lens aberration and veiling glare. Approximating the PSF as shift-invariant within each spatial patch ( Li et al., 2021a ; Luo et al., 2024a ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , we express the degradation independently for each color channel as: I d ​ e p = ( I c p ⊗ K p ) ⏟ I a ​ b p ⊙ T p + I g p , I_{de}^{p}=\underbrace{\left(I_{c}^{p}\otimes K^{p}\right)}_{I_{ab}^{p}}\odot T^{p}+I_{g}^{p}, (1) where p p indexes spatial patches, ⊗ \otimes denotes convolution, and ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. K p K^{p} is the local PSF, I a ​ b p I_{ab}^{p} is the aberrated patch, T p T^{p} models contrast attenuation, and I g p I_{g}^{p} represents additive glare ( Zhang et al., 2018b ; Shoshin & Shvets, 2021 ) . The color-channel index is omitted for clarity. Here, s s and t t denote the source and target domains, respectively, and N t ≪ N s N_{t}\ll N_{s} . Our objective is to first establish a reusable aberration correction foundation from 𝒟 s \mathcal{D}_{s} and then adapt it to target compound degradation using only the unpaired observations in 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} . LensBridge consists of two stages: (a) a reusable PSF-aware aberration correction foundation, where discrete degradation priors are constructed from LensLib PSFs and retrieved directly from aberrated observations; and (b) target-system compound degradation adaptation, where aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations separately condition the two adaptation branches. The shared one-step diffusion backbone and the frequency-guided pseudo decomposition mechanism are detailed in (c) and (d), respectively.

sections.heading: 3.2 Framework Overview
sections.text: As illustrated in Fig. 2 , LensBridge consists of two stages: establishing a reusable aberration correction foundation and adapting it to target-system compound degradation. We adopt SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , distilled from Stable Diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , as the one-step diffusion backbone. In Stage I, we construct discrete aberration priors from LensLib PSFs and train an image-based predictor to retrieve them from aberrated images. These priors condition low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) of the diffusion backbone. In Stage II, we estimate a shared target-system Fourier-amplitude statistic from a few unpaired target observations. Frequency-guided Degradation Completion (FDC) uses this statistic to construct target-like compound training pairs, while Frequency-guided Pseudo Decomposition (FPD) constructs aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations to condition separate adaptation branches.

sections.heading: 3.3 Stage I: Reusable Aberration Correction Foundation
sections.text: Aberration correction benefits from explicit PSF guidance, whereas target-system PSFs are typically unavailable at inference. We therefore construct a PSF-derived discrete prior space and train the Stage-I foundation in two phases. In Phase 1, PSF-guided Prior Construction , source-domain PSFs are encoded into discrete aberration priors to condition the diffusion backbone. In Phase 2, Blind Prior Retrieval , this prior space is fixed and an image-based predictor learns to retrieve the corresponding priors from aberrated observations by matching its predictions to PSF-derived representations during training, enabling PSF-aware correction without requiring PSFs at inference. Phase 1: PSF-guided Prior Construction. Following the discrete PSF representation strategy of FoundCAC ( Qian et al., 2026a ) , we employ vector quantization to construct the PSF-derived prior space. Specifically, a PSF encoder E PSF E_{\mathrm{PSF}} maps a PSF representation I PSF ∈ ℝ H × W × N p I_{\mathrm{PSF}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times N_{p}} to a continuous representation 𝐳 psf ∈ ℝ H z × W z × C z \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{z}\times W_{z}\times C_{z}} , which is quantized using a learnable codebook 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} to obtain 𝐳 psf q ∈ ℝ H z × W z × C z \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{z}\times W_{z}\times C_{z}} . The resulting codebook defines a discrete PSF-derived prior space for PSF-guided conditioning in Phase 1 and image-based retrieval in Phase 2, where image-predicted representations are matched to the corresponding PSF-derived priors during training. We regularize the encoder and codebook with the vector-quantization objective: ℒ VQ = ‖ sg ⁡ [ 𝐳 psf ] − 𝐳 psf q ‖ 2 2 + β ​ ‖ 𝐳 psf − sg ⁡ [ 𝐳 psf q ] ‖ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VQ}}=\left\|\operatorname{sg}[\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}]-\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\beta\left\|\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}-\operatorname{sg}[\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q}]\right\|_{2}^{2}, (2) where sg ⁡ [ ⋅ ] \operatorname{sg}[\cdot] denotes stop-gradient and β \beta controls the commitment term. The first term updates the selected codebook representations toward the encoder outputs, while the second encourages the encoder outputs to remain close to their assigned codes. Building on degradation-aware LoRA ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , we condition the low-rank update on PSF-derived discrete priors. For a pretrained weight 𝐖 0 ∈ ℝ d out × d in \mathbf{W}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} , standard LoRA uses two low-rank matrices 𝐁 ab ∈ ℝ d out × r \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ab}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r} and 𝐀 ab ∈ ℝ r × d in \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{ab}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} , where r ≪ min ⁡ ( d out , d in ) r\ll\min(d_{\mathrm{out}},d_{\mathrm{in}}) . An attention block maps the quantized prior 𝐳 psf q \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q} to a PSF-conditioned modulation matrix 𝐂 ab ∈ ℝ r × r \mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{ab}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r} , yielding: 𝐖 = 𝐖 0 + 𝐁 ab ​ 𝐂 ab ​ 𝐀 ab . \mathbf{W}=\mathbf{W}_{0}+\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ab}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{ab}}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{ab}}. (3) Compared with the standard LoRA update 𝐁 ab ​ 𝐀 ab \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ab}}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{ab}} , 𝐂 ab \mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{ab}} dynamically modulates the low-rank update according to the supplied aberration prior, enabling PSF-conditioned adaptation. Image reconstruction is supervised by a weighted combination of L1, perceptual, and adversarial losses, denoted as ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} . Jointly optimizing ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} and ℒ VQ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VQ}} encourages the discrete PSF-derived priors to provide effective conditioning for aberration restoration while regularizing their codebook assignments. Phase 2: Blind Prior Retrieval. To enable image-only inference while retaining PSF-derived degradation guidance, we train an RGB degradation predictor E pred E_{\mathrm{pred}} to retrieve the discrete priors established in Phase 1 directly from an aberrated image I a ​ b I_{ab} . To supervise this retrieval, the PSF encoder E PSF E_{\mathrm{PSF}} and codebook 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} are kept frozen. During training, the corresponding PSF representation is encoded and quantized to obtain the teacher prior 𝐳 psf q \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q} . A feature-matching loss ℒ FM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} ( Chen et al., 2022 ) aligns the predictor’s pre-quantization feature 𝐳 pred \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pred}} with 𝐳 psf q \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q} . The predicted feature is then quantized by the frozen codebook to obtain 𝐳 pred q \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pred}}^{q} for restoration conditioning. The retrieval stage is optimized with ℒ rec + ℒ FM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} . At inference, E pred E_{\mathrm{pred}} retrieves the aberration prior directly from the observed image without requiring the PSF.

sections.heading: 3.4 Stage II: Target-System Compound Degradation Adaptation
sections.text: In Stage I, we learn a reusable aberration correction foundation for PSF-induced degradation from LensLib. However, the source distribution does not cover target-specific factors ( i.e. , veiling glare) beyond the PSF space. The two degradations arise from different physical mechanisms and therefore exhibit distinct spectral responses. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (b), PSF-induced aberration modulates a broad frequency range, whereas the spatially smooth contamination of veiling glare mainly affects low-frequency amplitudes. We therefore estimate a shared target-system Fourier-amplitude statistic from a few unpaired observations to guide data-level degradation completion and model-level pseudo decomposition. Frequency-guided Degradation Completion. Directly transferring the Fourier amplitude of a single target image is unreliable because its spectrum is entangled with scene content. To obtain a target-system cue less sensitive to image-specific content, we aggregate Fourier-amplitude statistics over a few unpaired target observations. The resulting statistic is then used to complete the missing target degradation on LensLib aberrated images rather than regenerate the full degradation from clean images. Given a small target set 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} and an auxiliary clear-image collection 𝒟 clr \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{clr}} , we first compute their channel-wise mean Fourier amplitudes: 𝐀 ¯ 𝒟 c = 1 N 𝒟 ​ ∑ i = 1 N 𝒟 | ℱ ⁡ ( I i c ) | , 𝐆 tgt c = 𝐀 ¯ 𝒟 t c 𝐀 ¯ 𝒟 clr c + ϵ , \bar{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathcal{D}}^{c}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{D}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathcal{D}}}\left|\mathcal{F}(I_{i}^{c})\right|,\qquad\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}}^{c}=\frac{\bar{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathcal{D}_{t}}^{c}}{\bar{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{clr}}}^{c}+\epsilon}, (4) where ℱ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{F}(\cdot) denotes the centered 2D Fourier transform, c c indexes the color channel, and ϵ \epsilon ensures numerical stability. Averaging across images reduces image-specific spectral variation, allowing 𝐆 tgt \mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}} to capture the Fourier-amplitude discrepancy shared by the target observations. LensLib aberrated images I a ​ b s I_{ab}^{s} already contain diverse aberration characteristics that should be retained during target adaptation. We therefore modulate the Fourier amplitude of I a ​ b s I_{ab}^{s} using 𝐆 tgt \mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}} and retain its original phase. The low-frequency component of the modulated reconstruction is then combined with the original high-frequency component through wavelet decomposition ( Wang et al., 2024 ) : I ~ d ​ e s = 𝒲 H ​ ( I a ​ b s ) + 𝒲 L ​ ( ℱ − 1 ​ [ ( 𝐀 a ​ b s ⊙ 𝐆 tgt ) ​ e j ​ 𝚽 a ​ b s ] ) , \tilde{I}_{de}^{s}=\mathcal{W}_{H}(I_{ab}^{s})+\mathcal{W}_{L}\left(\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[\left(\mathbf{A}_{ab}^{s}\odot\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}}\right)e^{j\mathbf{\Phi}_{ab}^{s}}\right]\right), (5) where 𝐀 a ​ b s \mathbf{A}_{ab}^{s} and 𝚽 a ​ b s \mathbf{\Phi}_{ab}^{s} denote the Fourier amplitude and phase of I a ​ b s I_{ab}^{s} , respectively. During training, we further apply random spatial masks to modulate the transferred target characteristics, increasing spatial degradation diversity. Keeping the clean reference I c s I_{c}^{s} unchanged yields the target-like training pair ( I ~ d ​ e s , I c s ) (\tilde{I}_{de}^{s},I_{c}^{s}) , completing the missing target degradation while preserving the paired supervision from LensLib. Frequency-guided Pseudo Decomposition. Since aberration and veiling glare exhibit distinct degradation characteristics, a shared LoRA condition may entangle their adaptation signals. We therefore construct aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations to condition separate LoRA branches. For a compound-degraded image I d ​ e I_{de} , we suppress the target-specific low-frequency amplitude shift while retaining its original phase: I ^ a ​ b = ℱ − 1 ​ [ 𝐀 d ​ e Low ⁡ ( 𝐆 tgt ) + ϵ ​ e j ​ 𝚽 d ​ e ] , I ^ v ​ g = I d ​ e − I ^ a ​ b , \hat{I}_{ab}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[\frac{\mathbf{A}_{de}}{\operatorname{Low}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{tgt}})+\epsilon}e^{j\mathbf{\Phi}_{de}}\right],\qquad\hat{I}_{vg}=I_{de}-\hat{I}_{ab}, (6) where Low ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \operatorname{Low}(\cdot) preserves the target modulation within the low-frequency region and sets the remaining frequencies to one. The resulting I ^ a ​ b \hat{I}_{ab} and I ^ v ​ g \hat{I}_{vg} serve as aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations rather than physically exact degradation components, and are only used to provide factor-specific adaptation cues. The aberration-dominant observation I ^ a ​ b \hat{I}_{ab} is processed by the Stage-I degradation predictor, and the retrieved discrete aberration prior is mapped by the attention block to 𝐂 ab \mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{ab}} . In parallel, a lightweight VG encoder E VG E_{\mathrm{VG}} maps I ^ v ​ g \hat{I}_{vg} to the VG condition 𝐂 vg ∈ ℝ r × r \mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{vg}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r} . During Stage II, FDC-generated compound pairs are jointly used with the original LensLib aberration-only pairs for adaptation. The pretrained diffusion backbone and discrete codebook remain frozen during Stage II.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experiment Settings
sections.text: Datasets. We train the aberration correction foundation on LensLib ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , which provides paired aberration data and PSFs. For target adaptation and evaluation, we use the SL and MRL systems from DeVeiler ( Qian et al., 2026b ) , representing a large-aperture single lens and a metasurface-refractive hybrid lens, respectively. The Screen domain provides controlled monitor captures with 50 50 adaptation images and 42 / 25 42/25 paired test images for SL/MRL, while the Real domain contains in-the-wild captures with 50 50 adaptation images and 51 / 11 51/11 unpaired test images. All images are 1280 × 1920 1280\times 1920 . We further evaluate on the commercial minimalist lens CAYE 50 ​ mm 50\,\mathrm{mm} f / 1.4 f/1.4 and a nano-optics imaging system ( Tseng et al., 2021 ) . Our default unpaired-target setting uses only unpaired target images. We also consider a target aberration-paired setting with 170 / 125 170/125 additional aberration-only pairs for SL/MRL to compare with methods requiring target-specific supervision. For the generic clear-image collection 𝒟 clr \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{clr}} in Eq. 4 , we use the DIV2K training set. Implementation Details. We use SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) as the one-step restoration backbone, with rank- 16 16 aberration/VG LoRA branches in the VAE encoder and rank- 32 32 branches in the diffusion UNet. In Stage I, each phase is trained for 30 30 K iterations at 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} ; in Stage II, we adapt to each target system for 3 3 K iterations at 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} . Training uses 512 × 512 512\times 512 random crops with batch size 8 8 on an NVIDIA A800 GPU. Further details are provided in the supplementary material. sections.heading: 4.2 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
sections.text: We evaluate LensBridge under two target-adaptation settings. Our primary setting uses only unpaired compound-degraded target images and is also evaluated on additional optical systems. For fair comparison with DeVeiler ( Qian et al., 2026b ) and its benchmarked methods, we additionally consider the target aberration-paired setting. Unpaired target setting. In the primary setting, target adaptation uses only unpaired compound-degraded images. We compare against three groups of baselines. The first is Fast Two-Step ( Eboli et al., 2022 ) , a blind aberration correction method. The second comprises four general image restoration methods: DA-CLIP ( Luo et al., 2024b ) , AdaIR ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , FoundIR-v2 ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and FAPE-IR ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Their pretrained models are directly used for inference. The third comprises two domain adaptation methods: OmniLens ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) for aberration correction and DeVeiler ( Qian et al., 2026b ) for joint aberration and VG removal. Both are evaluated under the same unpaired-target setting as LensBridge . As shown in Tab. 1 , LensBridge performs favorably against existing methods on both Screen and Real domains. The gains are particularly consistent in LPIPS and no-reference image quality metrics, including over DeVeiler under the same setting. Visual comparisons in Figs. 3 and 4 further show that LensBridge restores fine details from aberration blur and color contrast degraded by veiling glare on both domains. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we address compound optical degradation involving co-existing aberration and veiling glare in simplified optical systems. We propose LensBridge , which adapts a reusable aberration correction foundation to target-specific compound degradation using only a few unpaired target observations, with a shared Fourier-amplitude statistic guiding both FDC and FPD. Experimental results across multiple optical systems demonstrate favorable restoration performance, effective few-shot adaptation, and applicability across different restoration backbones. We hope this work can facilitate efficient adaptation of reusable restoration foundations to diverse optical systems. Limitations and Future Work. LensBridge relies on the coverage of the LensLib foundation, and broader target-specific aberration priors could further improve unseen lens adaptation. The current VG adaptation uses frequency-guided degradation completion rather than a fully calibrated physical model, motivating future exploration of broader optical degradation foundations and physically grounded VG modeling under complex illumination.

sections.heading: Appendix A Additional Implementation Details
sections.text: Training Details. For the Stage-I foundation, training proceeds in two phases, with each phase optimized for 30 30 K iterations. In Phase 1, we jointly optimize the PSF encoder, discrete codebook, attention-based condition mapping module, and aberration-aware LoRA branch using ℒ rec + ℒ VQ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VQ}} . This establishes the PSF-derived discrete aberration prior space. In Phase 2, we freeze the PSF encoder and codebook and optimize the image-based degradation predictor together with the restoration adaptation modules. The frozen PSF branch provides teacher supervision through ℒ FM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} , encouraging the image-based predictor to retrieve consistent entries from the established codebook. The Phase-2 objective is ℒ rec + ℒ FM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} . For target-system adaptation, we initialize from the Stage-I model and adapt each optical system independently using a limited number of unpaired target observations. Compared with the foundation training, Stage-II requires lightweight optimization with only 3 3 K iterations for each target system. The pretrained SD-Turbo weights and discrete codebook remain frozen, while the image-based degradation predictor, attention-based condition mapping modules, VG encoder, and LoRA parameters of both branches are jointly optimized. The aberration branch is initialized from Stage I, while the VG branch is newly introduced. FDC-generated compound pairs are jointly sampled with the original LensLib aberration-only pairs during adaptation. Since the aberration-dominant observations generated by FPD are pseudo observations rather than physically exact aberration-only inputs, the feature matching loss is retained to preserve consistency with the Stage-I aberration prior space. The Stage-II objective combines the reconstruction loss and feature matching loss, i.e., ℒ II = ℒ rec + ℒ FM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{II}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} . sections.text: Visual Comparisons under the Unpaired-Target Setting. Figs. 11 and 12 provide additional visual comparisons on the Screen and Real domains, respectively. Across both SL and MRL systems, LensBridge better recovers fine structures degraded by aberration while reducing the contrast and color degradation associated with veiling glare. The improvements remain consistent across controlled screen captures and in-the-wild observations. Results on Additional Optical Systems. We provide additional results on the CAYE lens and nano-optics system, where the Stage-I foundation is independently adapted to each system using only a few unpaired degraded observations. As shown in Fig. 13 , Stage I already alleviates aberration-induced blur and recovers part of the image details, while subsequent target adaptation further improves contrast and color under compound degradation. The consistent behavior across both systems supports the applicability of the two-stage framework beyond the SL and MRL benchmarks. Visual Comparisons under the Target Aberration-Paired Setting. We provide additional visual comparisons under the target aberration-paired setting in Figs. 14 and 15 . Across both SL and MRL systems, LensBridge produces sharper structures and improved contrast compared with existing restoration and adaptation methods. These results complement the quantitative comparisons under the same setting, with consistent improvements across different optical systems. Additional Results on Real UDC Images. We further evaluate LensBridge on real UDC images from Feng et al. (2021) . UDC images exhibit severe contrast attenuation and haze-like appearance caused by complex optical artifacts, providing an additional out-of-distribution case beyond the current LensLib degradation distribution. As shown in Fig. 16 , the method improves global contrast and visibility across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes, while fine diffraction artifacts remain challenging due to the absence of diffraction-aware PSFs in the current LensLib distribution. This experiment provides an additional qualitative evaluation of the proposed foundation-to-compound adaptation paradigm under unseen optical degradations. Failure Cases and Future Work. Fig. 17 shows two representative challenging cases. For the SL system, fine high-frequency structures such as small text remain difficult to reconstruct accurately, partly due to latent-space compression and the absence of dedicated high-frequency restoration designs. For the MRL system, severe overexposure produces saturated regions with substantial information loss, preventing faithful recovery of the missing content. Future work will explore dedicated high-frequency restoration modules, more robust handling of severely saturated observations. Affiliation: Zhejiang University Abstract Simplified optical systems often exhibit residual lens aberrations and Veiling Glare (VG), resulting in spatially varying blur and contrast reduction. Large-scale Lens Libraries (LensLib) enable reusable aberration correction models by covering diverse Point Spread Functions (PSFs), but their aberration-only training distribution does not include target-specific veiling glare. Extending such foundations to compound degradation is challenging because realistic target-system compound pairs are difficult to obtain. To address this challenge, we propose LensBridge , a two-stage framework that first establishes a reusable aberration correction foundation and then adapts it to compound optical degradation using only a few unpaired target observations. In Stage I, we build a PSF-aware one-step diffusion foundation by constructing discrete degradation priors from LensLib PSFs and learning to retrieve them directly from aberrated images, enabling PSF-aware correction without requiring explicit PSF at inference. In Stage II, we adapt this foundation to compound degradation through frequency-domain guidance. Our analysis suggests that aberrations affect a broad frequency range, whereas additional veiling glare exhibits stronger low-frequency amplitude variations, motivating a shared target-domain Fourier-amplitude statistic. At the data level, Frequency-guided Degradation Completion (FDC) transfers target low-frequency characteristics to LensLib aberrated images while preserving aberration structures to synthesize compound training pairs; at the model level, Frequency-guided Pseudo Decomposition (FPD) forms aberration- and VG-dominant pseudo observations to condition separate adaptation branches. Extensive experiments across multiple optical systems demonstrate that LensBridge effectively extends reusable aberration correction foundations to joint aberration correction and veiling glare removal without target-system paired supervision. All code will be available at https://github.com/XiaolongQian/LensBridge . 1 Introduction Simplified optical designs enable compact imaging systems for mobile photography ( Chen et al., 2021a ; Chen et al., 2023 ) and emerging meta-optical devices ( Li et al., 2021b ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , but often leave substantial residual lens aberrations. Meanwhile, surface imperfections and non-ideal coatings can also induce diffuse stray-light scattering, manifested as Veiling Glare (VG) ( Qian et al., 2026b ) . Lens aberrations introduce spatially varying blur and chromatic dispersion, while veiling glare causes diffuse luminance contamination and contrast reduction. Their coexistence results in compound optical degradation , motivating computational restoration capable of addressing both effects. Existing computational restoration for optical degradation has primarily focused on lens aberrations. Conventional learning-based approaches typically rely on target-system synthetic pairs generated from Point Spread Functions (PSFs) ( Chen et al., 2021a ; Chen et al., 2021b ) . As illustrated by the synthetic-to-real paradigm in Fig. 1 (a), such models are trained on target-lens synthetic data and then transferred to real aberrated images ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Acquiring target-lens PSFs and constructing synthetic training pairs for new optical system make deployment costly. Pretraining on large-scale Lens Libraries (LensLib) alleviates this burden by learning reusable correction models across diverse aberration distributions ( Gong et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2026a ) . Among these methods, OmniLens ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) follows the foundation-to-specific paradigm in Fig. 1 (a), adapting a LensLib foundation to unseen lenses with unpaired aberrated images and a dark-channel prior. Figure 1: Motivation for LensBridge . (a) Comparison of optical adaptation paradigms in terms of source pretraining and target degradation. LensBridge adapts a reusable aberration correction foundation to target compound degradation using only unpaired target images. (b) In the illustrated example, aberration induces broadband amplitude changes, whereas the additional veiling glare produces predominantly low-frequency amplitude changes and a smaller phase-swap reconstruction error in the illustrated example, motivating the frequency-guided designs of FDC and FPD. However, these reusable foundations are learned within the aberration-only degradation space of LensLib and therefore cannot account for veiling glare. Extending them to compound degradation remains challenging, as physically accurate veiling glare simulation requires optomechanical models and computationally expensive non-sequential ray tracing ( Raskar et al., 2008 ; Hullin et al., 2011 ) , making reliable target-system compound pairs difficult to obtain. A recent solution is target-specific compound degradation synthesis. DeVeiler ( Qian et al., 2026b ) follows the target-specific-to-compound paradigm in Fig. 1 (a), using target-lens aberration pairs and unpaired compound observations to synthesize realistic lens-specific compound degradations for joint restoration. However, its synthesis remains tailored to each target system rather than reusing an aberration correction foundation across lenses. In contrast, we pursue a foundation-to-compound paradigm, where reusable aberration knowledge is retained from LensLib and only a few unpaired compound observations are required to adapt the foundation to a new optical system. To enable such adaptation, we examine the two degradation mechanisms in the frequency domain, where PSF-induced blur and diffuse stray-light effects exhibit different spectral responses. PSF-induced aberration modifies image content across a broad frequency range, whereas veiling glare primarily affects low-frequency amplitude components, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (b). This distinction motivates using target-domain low-frequency amplitude statistics to characterize the degradation information missing from the aberration-only foundation. We therefore propose LensBridge , a two-stage framework that first establishes a reusable aberration correction foundation and then adapts it to compound optical degradation. In Stage I, we establish a PSF-aware one-step diffusion foundation for reusable aberration correction. LensLib PSFs are encoded into a discrete degradation prior space, while image-conditioned retrieval enables the corresponding priors to be inferred directly from aberrated observations. The retrieved priors condition the diffusion restoration backbone, retaining PSF-aware degradation guidance without requiring explicit PSFs at inference. In Stage II, we adapt this foundation to target compound degradation using only a few unpaired target observations. Based on the above frequency distinction, we estimate a shared target-system Fourier-amplitude statistic to guide adaptation at both the data and model levels. At the data level, Frequency-guided Degradation Completion (FDC) performs data-level adaptation by transferring target-domain low-frequency degradation characteristics to LensLib aberrated images while preserving their aberration-related structures and clean counterparts, thereby constructing target-like compound training pairs without learning an additional degradation generator. At the model level, Frequency-guided Pseudo Decomposition (FPD) uses the same frequency statistic to construct aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations, allowing the two adaptation branches to model their distinct degradation characteristics separately. Together, FDC provides target-like training supervision, while FPD separately conditions the aberration and VG adaptation branches. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose LensBridge , a two-stage framework that first establishes a reusable LensLib-based aberration correction foundation and then adapts it to compound aberration and veiling-glare degradation using only a few unpaired target observations. • We introduce FDC and FPD, which leverage a shared target-domain Fourier-amplitude statistic to construct target-like compound training pairs and aberration-/VG-dominant pseudo observations, respectively. • Extensive experiments across multiple optical systems demonstrate the effectiveness of LensBridge for joint aberration correction and veiling glare removal. 2 Related Work Lens Aberration Correction. Computational Aberration Correction (CAC) aims to restore images degraded by residual lens aberrations. Early approaches relied on deconvolution or PSF-based inverse filtering ( Wiener, 1949 ; Fish et al., 1995 ; Schuler et al., 2012 ) . With the emergence of deep learning, learning-based CAC methods ( Chen et al., 2021a ; Chen et al., 2021b ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Mandal et al., 2025 ) learn restoration mappings from simulated optical degradations and achieve improved performance. However, these methods typically depend on lens-specific simulation pipelines and suffer from limited generalization to unseen optical systems. Recent works explore reusable CAC models through large-scale lens library pre-training ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2026a ) , where diverse aberration distributions improve cross-lens generalization and support adaptation to new lenses. Nevertheless, existing LensLib-based frameworks remain confined to PSF-induced aberrations and do not address compound degradations involving veiling glare. Veiling Glare Removal. Veiling glare is a diffuse degradation caused by stray-light scattering inside optical systems, leading to luminance contamination and contrast reduction. Unlike lens flare, which typically appears as localized structures such as bright spots and streaks ( Wu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Dai et al., 2024 ; Vasluianu et al., 2024 ; Zhu & Lee, 2025 ) , veiling glare is spatially distributed and dominated by low-frequency variations. Traditional approaches rely on physical modeling or image decomposition, including Glare Spread Function (GSF) based inverse filtering ( Talvala et al., 2007 ) and glare-component decomposition ( Zhang et al., 2018b ) , but often require restrictive assumptions, calibration, or multiple observations. Recent data-driven methods ( Shoshin & Shvets, 2021 ) use simplified flare or scattering models for training-data synthesis, leaving a substantial gap from lens-specific real degradations. DeVeiler ( Qian et al., 2026b ) addresses this limitation through target-specific compound degradation synthesis, but its degradation modeling must be repeated for each new optical system. In contrast, LensBridge reuses a LensLib-based aberration correction foundation and adapts it to compound degradation using only unpaired target observations. Frequency-Guided Degradation Adaptation. Frequency-domain statistics have been widely explored for domain adaptation and image restoration. FDA transfers low-frequency Fourier amplitudes between source and target domains for unsupervised semantic segmentation ( Yang & Soatto, 2020 ) , while FCA exploits frequency consistency to reduce the synthetic-to-real gap in real-world super-resolution ( Ji et al., 2021 ) . Frequency-aware dehazing methods further exploit amplitude-spectrum discrepancies between synthetic and real degradations for adaptation or restoration ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . These methods demonstrate the effectiveness of frequency statistics for characterizing domain shifts, but mainly use them for global source-to-target alignment or adaptation within a single degradation type. In contrast, LensBridge uses an aggregated target-domain Fourier-amplitude statistic to complete the missing target degradation characteristics associated with VG while preserving the existing LensLib aberration structure, and further reuses the same statistic to construct aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations. 3 Methodology 3.1 Problem Formulation We aim to recover a latent clean image I c I_{c} from a compound-degraded image I d ​ e I_{de} captured by a target optical system. Following ( Qian et al., 2026b ) , we model the joint effects of spatially varying lens aberration and veiling glare. Approximating the PSF as shift-invariant within each spatial patch ( Li et al., 2021a ; Luo et al., 2024a ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , we express the degradation independently for each color channel as: I d ​ e p = ( I c p ⊗ K p ) ⏟ I a ​ b p ⊙ T p + I g p , I_{de}^{p}=\underbrace{\left(I_{c}^{p}\otimes K^{p}\right)}_{I_{ab}^{p}}\odot T^{p}+I_{g}^{p}, (1) where p p indexes spatial patches, ⊗ \otimes denotes convolution, and ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. K p K^{p} is the local PSF, I a ​ b p I_{ab}^{p} is the aberrated patch, T p T^{p} models contrast attenuation, and I g p I_{g}^{p} represents additive glare ( Zhang et al., 2018b ; Shoshin & Shvets, 2021 ) . The color-channel index is omitted for clarity. We use a LensLib source dataset 𝒟 s = { ( I a ​ b , i s , I c , i s ) } i = 1 N s \mathcal{D}_{s}=\{(I_{ab,i}^{s},I_{c,i}^{s})\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}} , with a corresponding PSF for each pair, and a small set of unpaired compound-degraded target images 𝒟 t = { I d ​ e , j t } j = 1 N t \mathcal{D}_{t}=\{I_{de,j}^{t}\}_{j=1}^{N_{t}} . Here, s s and t t denote the source and target domains, respectively, and N t ≪ N s N_{t}\ll N_{s} . Our objective is to first establish a reusable aberration correction foundation from 𝒟 s \mathcal{D}_{s} and then adapt it to target compound degradation using only the unpaired observations in 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} . Figure 2: Overview of LensBridge . LensBridge consists of two stages: (a) a reusable PSF-aware aberration correction foundation, where discrete degradation priors are constructed from LensLib PSFs and retrieved directly from aberrated observations; and (b) target-system compound degradation adaptation, where aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations separately condition the two adaptation branches. The shared one-step diffusion backbone and the frequency-guided pseudo decomposition mechanism are detailed in (c) and (d), respectively. 3.2 Framework Overview As illustrated in Fig. 2 , LensBridge consists of two stages: establishing a reusable aberration correction foundation and adapting it to target-system compound degradation. We adopt SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , distilled from Stable Diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , as the one-step diffusion backbone. In Stage I, we construct discrete aberration priors from LensLib PSFs and train an image-based predictor to retrieve them from aberrated images. These priors condition low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) of the diffusion backbone. In Stage II, we estimate a shared target-system Fourier-amplitude statistic from a few unpaired target observations. Frequency-guided Degradation Completion (FDC) uses this statistic to construct target-like compound training pairs, while Frequency-guided Pseudo Decomposition (FPD) constructs aberration-dominant and VG-dominant pseudo observations to condition separate adaptation branches. 3.3 Stage I: Reusable Aberration Correction Foundation Aberration correction benefits from explicit PSF guidance, whereas target-system PSFs are typically unavailable at inference. We therefore construct a PSF-derived discrete prior space and train the Stage-I foundation in two phases. In Phase 1, PSF-guided Prior Construction , source-domain PSFs are encoded into discrete aberration priors to condition the diffusion backbone. In Phase 2, Blind Prior Retrieval , this prior space is fixed and an image-based predictor learns to retrieve the corresponding priors from aberrated observations by matching its predictions to PSF-derived representations during training, enabling PSF-aware correction without requiring PSFs at inference. Phase 1: PSF-guided Prior Construction. Following the discrete PSF representation strategy of FoundCAC ( Qian et al., 2026a ) , we employ vector quantization to construct the PSF-derived prior space. Specifically, a PSF encoder E PSF E_{\mathrm{PSF}} maps a PSF representation I PSF ∈ ℝ H × W × N p I_{\mathrm{PSF}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times N_{p}} to a continuous representation 𝐳 psf ∈ ℝ H z × W z × C z \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{z}\times W_{z}\times C_{z}} , which is quantized using a learnable codebook 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} to obtain 𝐳 psf q ∈ ℝ H z × W z × C z \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{z}\times W_{z}\times C_{z}} . The resulting codebook defines a discrete PSF-derived prior space for PSF-guided conditioning in Phase 1 and image-based retrieval in Phase 2, where image-predicted representations are matched to the corresponding PSF-derived priors during training. We regularize the encoder and codebook with the vector-quantization objective: ℒ VQ = ‖ sg ⁡ [ 𝐳 psf ] − 𝐳 psf q ‖ 2 2 + β ​ ‖ 𝐳 psf − sg ⁡ [ 𝐳 psf q ] ‖ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VQ}}=\left\|\operatorname{sg}[\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}]-\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\beta\left\|\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}-\operatorname{sg}[\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{psf}}^{q}]\right\|_{2}^{2}, (2) where sg ⁡ [ ⋅ ] \operatorname{sg}[\cdot] denotes stop-gradient and β \beta controls the commitment term. The first term updates the selected codebook representations toward the encoder outputs, while the second encourages the encoder outputs to remain close to their assigned codes. Building on degradation-aware LoRA ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , we condition the low-rank update on PSF-derived discrete priors. For a pretrained weight 𝐖 0 ∈ ℝ d out × d in \mathbf{W}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} , standard LoRA uses two low-rank matrices 𝐁 ab ∈ ℝ d out × r \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ab}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r} and 𝐀 ab ∈ ℝ r × d in \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{ab}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} , where r ≪ min ⁡ ( d out , d in ) r\ll\min(d_{\mathrm{out}},d_{\mathrm{in}}) . However, the source distribution does not cover target-specific factors ( i.e. , veiling glare) beyond the PSF space. The two degradations arise from different physical mechanisms and therefore exhibit distinct spectral responses. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (b), PSF-induced aberration modulates a broad frequency range, whereas the spatially smooth contamination of veiling glare mainly affects low-frequency amplitudes. We therefore estimate a shared target-system Fourier-amplitude statistic from a few unpaired observations to guide data-level degradation completion and model-level pseudo decomposition. We propose LensBridge , which adapts a reusable aberration correction foundation to target-specific compound degradation using only a few unpaired target observations, with a shared Fourier-amplitude statistic guiding both FDC and FPD. Experimental results across multiple optical systems demonstrate favorable restoration performance, effective few-shot adaptation, and applicability across different restoration backbones. We hope this work can facilitate efficient adaptation of reusable restoration foundations to diverse optical systems. Limitations and Future Work. LensBridge relies on the coverage of the LensLib foundation, and broader target-specific aberration priors could further improve unseen lens adaptation. The current VG adaptation uses frequency-guided degradation completion rather than a fully calibrated physical model, motivating future exploration of broader optical degradation foundations and physically grounded VG modeling under complex illumination.
